summary: Describes privacy extensions for IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration. Rather than deriving the interface identifier from a hardware identifier, a node can generate temporary changing ones to make tracking harder. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 8981.

eli5.summary: If your address always includes your device's fixed name, people can follow you around. This lets your device use changing nicknames.

questions: how to stop ipv6 address tracking
how often do ipv6 temporary addresses change
are ipv6 temporary addresses on by default
subtitle: How an IPv6 device can use short-lived random addresses so that it is harder to track across networks and over time.

tldr.problem: IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration can build the interface identifier from a hardware address, so the same identifier follows a device everywhere it connects and lets observers correlate its activity.
tldr.mechanism: A node generates extra temporary addresses from randomized interface identifiers made with a hash, uses them for outgoing connections, and replaces them regularly while the normal public addresses keep working.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4941 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 3041. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8981.

today: RFC 4941 is a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 3041 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8981, so RFC 8981 is the document to read for the current specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
With IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, an interface that has a built-in IEEE identifier (a link-layer MAC address) typically derives a 64-bit interface identifier from it. That identifier is appended to a prefix to form the 128-bit address. Because the identifier is likely globally unique and never changes, it can be used to tell that different addresses belong to the same device.

This RFC extends stateless address autoconfiguration so that nodes also generate global scope addresses from interface identifiers that change over time. This makes it harder for eavesdroppers and information collectors to link different transactions to the same node.
sections.eli5: Your device builds its address using a name stamped on its hardware. This note lets it build addresses from made-up names that change.

sections.title: The Tracking Problem
sections.content:
Any time a fixed identifier is used in many contexts, unrelated activity can be correlated. Two kinds of observers can do it: someone on the path who sees addresses in packets, and someone who reads the logs of the peers a node has talked to. Addresses appear in the clear even when the payload is encrypted. A laptop that moves between home and office keeps the same interface identifier while the prefix changes, so it can be followed from place to place.

The RFC is frank about the limits. The network prefix is also a constant identifier, so with a single node on a prefix changing only the interface identifier does not help. A DNS name that stays the same is a constant identifier too. And payload contents, packet sizes and timing can still allow correlation, so temporary addresses do not prevent that. It also says the method is believed to be ineffective against sophisticated traffic analysis.
sections.eli5: Even if your letters are sealed, the return address is visible. If the same part of the return address is on every letter, someone can spot that all the letters come from you.

sections.title: Generating Randomized Identifiers
sections.content:
The default method uses a 64-bit history value and the MD5 hash. The node appends the history value to the interface identifier it would normally have, computes the MD5 digest, and takes the leftmost 64 bits with bit 6 set to zero, marking the identifier as locally significant. If the result is on a list of reserved identifiers, or already in use on the device, the node restarts using the rightmost 64 bits of the digest as the new history value. Otherwise it saves the identifier and stores the rightmost 64 bits as the next history value.

On the first boot, the history value should be a random value that is hard to guess. Without stable storage, the initial value should be random too, and may be built from machine-specific configuration data plus random data. A node MAY use a different algorithm than MD5. The RFC notes that Cryptographically Generated Addresses are unsuitable here, since they need a public key that would itself identify the node and are costly to regenerate.
sections.eli5: The device mixes a secret number with its own name, stirs it up with a blender-like math trick, and keeps a piece of the result as its made-up name. Next time it mixes in what is left over.

sections.title: Temporary Addresses and Their Lifetimes
sections.content:
When a Router Advertisement carries a global prefix with the autoconfiguration (A) bit set, the node processes it as usual and SHOULD also create a temporary address by appending its current randomized identifier to the prefix. Lifetimes are capped: the valid lifetime is the lower of the public address's value and TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME, and the preferred lifetime is the lower of the public address's value and TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus DESYNC_FACTOR. Duplicate address detection (DAD) MUST be run on every generated address, with up to TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES new identifiers tried before the node logs a system error and stops generating temporary addresses for that interface.

Temporary addresses are used for outgoing connections only. When one becomes deprecated, a new one MUST be generated, starting REGEN_ADVANCE before the old one is deprecated. A deprecated address may still serve connections already open. When an interface attaches to a new link, a new randomized identifier SHOULD be generated at once, so addresses on different links are hard to connect.
sections.eli5: Your device keeps its regular address for people who call you, and uses a throwaway nickname when it calls others. Every day or so it swaps in a new nickname, a little before the old one retires.

sections.title: Deployment and Side Effects
sections.content:
Devices MUST give end users a way to turn temporary addresses on or off, and SHOULD let trusted administrators do so, including per prefix range, for example disabling them for Unique Local prefixes. Because temporary addresses can disrupt some applications, they SHOULD be disabled by default; this was a change from RFC 3041.

Changing identifiers has costs. Operators find troubleshooting harder when packet traces show shifting addresses. Some servers insist on a reverse DNS name for the client and check that it maps back to the same address, and clients with temporary addresses may be refused. Applications that expect an address to last, or to be shared across several sessions, may also break if an address expires. Changing addresses very often could also hurt performance because of address lookups and multicast group membership.
sections.eli5: Nicknames are great for privacy, but the school office cannot find you as easily when something goes wrong, and some clubs only let in people with a known name. So the nicknames start switched off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The only security concern raised is for ingress filtering, which networks use to block spoofed source addresses in distributed denial of service attacks. In a network with many nodes, new temporary addresses are created at a fairly high rate. That can make it hard for ingress filters to distinguish legitimately changing temporary addresses from spoofed in-prefix addresses that use a topologically correct prefix and a non-existent interface ID.

The RFC suggests that this can be handled with per-address access control at the network egress point. The privacy limits described earlier, such as payload-based correlation, are also part of the honest picture of what the extension protects against.
sections.eli5: When people keep changing their nicknames, a guard at the gate has a harder time telling a real visitor from someone faking a name. Checking each name at the exit door helps.
